items.title: [New Atlas] Global warming may have prevented a return to the ice age 2,000 years ago
items.content_html:
Earth’s persistently frozen poles mean the last ice age never really came to an end. What we think of as the mammoth-romping, Neanderthal-stomping chapter of geological history was technically a glacial maximum, one our planet would now be returning to if not for our love of burning coal, according to a recently published study.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] James Webb discovers a scorching lava planet with a “giant sunscreen”
items.content_html: A scorching lava planet 280 light-years away has surprised astronomers by apparently maintaining a thick atmosphere despite conditions that should have stripped it away billions of years ago. James Webb Space Telescope observations suggest that TOI-561 b reflects about 75% of incoming starlight, possibly because of mineral clouds that act like a giant sunscreen. The planet may also be continually replenishing its atmosphere through gases released from a global ocean of molten rock.

items.title: [sciencealert.com] Triassic armored amphibian fossils point to life entirely at sea
items.content_html: Researchers have described Gerrothorax maritimus, an armored amphibian that may have lived its entire life in the sea about 237 million years ago. The claim rests on two nearly complete skeletons found in marine deposits in Guizhou, China, more than 30 kilometers from nearby islands. Their preserved limbs and strontium isotope signatures are consistent with the animals having lived and grown in seawater. The study appeared in Nature Ecology & Evolution on Oct. 26. The roughly 74-centimeter-long animal had a flattened body covered in bony armor. Researchers propose that the armor limited water exchange through its skin, while its gills and digestive tract may have helped it cope with salt. Its skull shape suggests it waited on the seafloor and sucked in prey. No living amphibian is known to live exclusively in the ocean, and fewer than 2% of modern amphibian species show any salt tolerance.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Chinese scientists discover “D-rex,” a giant fungus with roots stretching back 65 million years
items.content_html: Scientists have discovered a giant new fungus in China that grows up to 20 inches tall and weighs nearly five pounds, making it the largest known of its kind. Dubbed “D-rex,” its evolutionary lineage appears to have emerged shortly after the dinosaurs went extinct, raising intriguing questions about how that ancient catastrophe may have shaped its evolution.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] AI detects “invisible” signs of pancreatic cancer years before diagnosis
items.content_html: A powerful new AI system could help doctors detect pancreatic cancer years before it becomes visible on conventional scans. The technology, called REDMOD, identified hidden warning signs an average of 475 days before diagnosis and was nearly twice as sensitive as experienced radiologists. By spotting cancer-related changes at their earliest stages, it could dramatically improve the chances of successful treatment for one of the deadliest forms of cancer.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Scientists overcome a hidden obstacle to more powerful quantum computers
items.content_html: Scientists have discovered a way to operate multiple silicon qubits simultaneously with remarkable accuracy, overcoming a major challenge in scaling up quantum computers. Their new technique maintained accuracy of approximately 99.9% even when all five qubits were running at once, opening the door to larger and more powerful quantum processors.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] New evidence suggests spinosaurus spent most of its life underwater
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

Millions of years after animals first conquered land, some took an extraordinary evolutionary U-turn and returned to the water. Using machine learning and thousands of fossil measurements, Yale scientists have uncovered surprising clues about which prehistoric creatures truly became aquatic. Their findings suggest that Spinosaurus spent most of its life underwater, while some ancient marine reptiles previously thought to be fully aquatic actually spent considerable time on land.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Scientists discover how pancreatic cancer rewrites its DNA to escape treatment
items.content_html: Scientists have discovered how pancreatic cancer cells continually reshape their genetic makeup to become more aggressive, spread, and evade treatment. In laboratory experiments, blocking a key gene reversed some of these dangerous changes, revealing a potential new way to fight the deadly disease.

items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Scientists have proposed a way to detect “mirror life,” a hypothetical form of life that could pose serious risks to humans, animals, and ecosystems if artificially created. Using special fluorescent molecules and a type of polarized light also used in 3D movie technology, researchers believe they could distinguish ordinary organisms from their mirror-image counterparts.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Astronomers uncover a mysterious magnetic web above the Sun
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

The Sun’s seemingly peaceful regions are hiding a surprisingly complex magnetic world. Using a balloon-borne telescope high above Earth, scientists discovered delicate, thread-like magnetic structures woven through the solar atmosphere, apparently shaped by twisting motions on the Sun’s surface. They also mapped magnetic fields inside towering jets of solar material, revealing how those fields change with height.

items.title: [ouest-france.fr] OpenAI publishes 722 AI-generated math manuscripts, prompting research debate
items.content_html: OpenAI published 722 mathematical manuscripts generated by an advanced AI system in early October, weeks after announcing that AI agents had solved the Navier–Stokes problem, which describes fluid motion. Researchers have debated the reliability of the proofs, credit for the research and whether answers without clear explanations count as mathematical progress. Terence Tao, a mathematics professor at the University of California, Los Angeles, said companies had used open problems to evaluate AI models and released poorly polished results. Two researchers who had spent a year working on Navier–Stokes with OpenAI tools said the company used their work to develop its reasoning. Other mathematicians say AI can accelerate searches but stress the importance of selecting worthwhile questions and explaining proofs. Ken Duffy, a mathematics professor at Northeastern, said research depends on “finding a good question to ask”.

items.title: [sciencenews.org] Ancient viral DNA silences chimp gene linked to early brain development
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Researchers at Lund University report that DNA left by an ancient retrovirus, PTERV1, silences LINC00662, a gene active in human brain development, in chimpanzees. In lab-grown brain organoids, switching off the gene reduced the activity of genes involved in neuron development and connections; removing the viral sequence from chimpanzee stem cells restored LINC00662 activity. The researchers caution that the experiments cannot establish effects on whole-brain development, abilities or behavior. The study appeared in Science Advances on October 23. The team says it will investigate whether other viral remnants had similar effects and whether such sequences are linked to brain diseases.

items.title: [zmescience.com] Protein evidence identifies Chinese fossils as Denisovans, revealing likely facial traits
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Researchers have identified human fossils from Xujiayao in northern China as Denisovans using ancient proteins, then compared their bones with other remains to infer the group’s likely appearance. The fossils suggest Denisovans had low, backward-sloping foreheads, heavy brow ridges and broad, relatively flat faces, with features distinct from those of Neanderthals. The team recovered a Denisovan-linked collagen variant from two fossils with no surviving DNA. The Xujiayao collection includes 20 specimens excavated decades ago. The researchers argue that some Chinese fossils previously assigned to separate human groups may instead represent variation within the Denisovan lineage. That classification remains uncertain for specimens identified only by resemblance, and researchers say additional samples would help test it.
